channel.title: Jay Rosen's Internet Archive
channel.description: Archive of Jay Rosen's journalism scholarship, including articles, essays, social posts, and the 1986 dissertation "The Impossible Press"
channel.generator: Jay Rosen's Internet Archive RSS Generator

item.title: Margaret Sullivan grades midterm coverage
item.description: Rosen recommends Margaret Sullivan's assessment of midterm press coverage, noting that she explicitly uses the frame of stakes rather than odds.

item.title: Exposure and accountability as different political tasks
item.description: Rosen connects his earlier thread about distinctions in media criticism with Brian Beutler's argument that exposure is not accountability.

item.title: An emergency setting for Trump coverage
item.description: Rosen revisits his March 2020 PressThink essay written in the voice of a newsroom editor explaining a different approach to Trump coverage.

item.title: Helping the web archive itself
item.description: Rosen shares Dave Winer's call to help the web preserve itself and links to Jay Rosen's Internet Archive as his own contribution.

item.title: Ellison, Trump, and access for CNN
item.description: Rosen highlights David Ellison's stated support for restoring CNN's access to cover Trump and argues that this conflict should lead coverage of the new CNN.

item.title: Not the odds but the stakes in election coverage
item.description: Rosen restates his proposed organizing principle for election coverage: Focus on consequences for American democracy rather than winning probabilities. He refers back to September 11, 2023.

item.title: Where can readers find the citizens agenda itself?
item.description: After James Brooks describes an Alaska Beacon decision guided by a citizens agenda, Rosen asks where the site presents the agenda itself rather than commentary about it.

item.title: David Ellison's claims about truth, trust, and Trump
item.description: Rosen highlights Status's questions at David Ellison's press conference and the tension between Ellison's appeal to truth and trust and his account of Trump's enthusiasm.

item.title: The argument is not that earlier criticism never existed
item.description: Responding to a comment about earlier work by Ornstein and Mann, Rosen rejects the suggestion that the discussion claims these ideas had never been expressed before.

item.title: A revised recommendation of Polarization Is Not the Problem
item.description: Rosen again recommends Lilliana Mason's argument about polarization and both-sides journalism and invites readers' reactions.

item.title: An earlier Bluesky example of the same journalism problem
item.description: In the discussion of Polarization Is Not the Problem, Rosen links to a 2024 Bluesky post that presents part of his earlier formulation.

item.description: A 3-post Bluesky thread by Jay Rosen.

item.title: The Daily Beast's character-driven election coverage
item.description: Rosen argues that the Daily Beast's character-driven approach offers an alternative to the view from nowhere, while making Trump its central character also brings costs.

item.title: A PressThink example from before Trump
item.description: In a discussion about journalism's deterioration before Trump, Rosen links to a December 2006 PressThink post as an earlier example moving in the same direction.

item.title: An older PressThink post in a discussion of political advertising
item.description: Replying in a discussion of television stations' obligations around Trump-related advertising, Rosen offers a November 2004 PressThink post while acknowledging that it does not answer the precise question.

item.title: A reporter's account of Trump's lying
item.description: Rosen recommends a Canadian reporter's CNN account of studying Trump's rhetoric, public reactions to his lying, and the way it is covered.

item.title: Why the press pool fights matter
item.description: Rosen recommends a Washington Post column, shared by Brian Stelter, as an explanation of why disputes over press pool access matter.

item.title: Send the interns and the press pool boycott
item.description: Quoting On the Media's question about why journalists took so long to reconsider their norms, Rosen points to his January 2017 PressThink essay Send the interns.

item.title: The problem of an unbiased detector of newsroom bias
item.description: Rosen questions the idea of an unbiased measure of newsroom bias in a Paramount agreement discussed by CNN.

item.title: An unbiased hat does not settle judgments about commentators
item.description: Replying to Alex's suggested list of commentators in the discussion of newsroom bias, Rosen uses irony to show how an assertion of impartiality does not settle the underlying judgment.

item.title: Josh Marshall on platform audiences
item.description: Rosen shares Josh Marshall's distinction between Bluesky users' expectations and the belief among some X users that they encounter a representative population. Rosen corrects Marshall's name in a later post.

item.title: Correcting Josh Marshall's name
item.description: Quoting his earlier post about platform audiences, Rosen corrects the attribution from the misspelled name in that post to Josh Marshall.

item.title: A press pool without shared presidential video
item.description: Rosen shares Brian Stelter's account of a presidential appearance without a television camera supplying footage to the wider press corps.

item.title: Revisiting Send the interns
item.description: Rosen recommends his PressThink essay Send the interns, published on the second day of the first Trump White House.

item.title: The propaganda risks of a media merger
item.description: Rosen shares an argument that combining entertainment and news in a large propaganda structure could make it especially effective.

item.title: News marketing and the promise of insider access
item.description: In the opening post of a two-part argument, Rosen questions news subscription imagery that promises readers greater access to an inner circle.

item.title: Two meanings of journalism's inner circle
item.description: Continuing his post about news subscription imagery, Rosen distinguishes reporting that makes readers feel present from a paid promise of knowledge withheld from others.

item.title: Commercialization, gatekeepers, and internet distribution
item.description: Asked whether insider journalism began with Evans and Novak, Rosen describes a longer commercialization process. He argues that media companies' control of distribution changed when the internet offered different terms.

item.title: Which newsrooms make up the national mainstream press?
item.description: Rosen revisits his 2016 PressThink essay on party asymmetry and notes that its definition of the national mainstream press would differ today.

item.title: A community's bond with the Lexington Herald-Leader
item.description: Rosen recommends a city council member's speech after newsroom cuts at the Lexington Herald-Leader as evidence of a newspaper's community bond and independence.

item.title: The 60 Minutes premiere and its audience decline
item.description: Rosen shares Status's comparison of the 60 Minutes premiere audience with the previous year and points to an accompanying view of the decline.

item.title: Margaret Sullivan on midterm stakes
item.description: Rosen shares Margaret Sullivan's plan to track midterm coverage with greater attention to consequences and less attention to winning probabilities.

item.title: Brian Williams on normalization in news coverage
item.description: Rosen shares a video in which Brian Williams responds to a question about extremism reaching public life. Rosen highlights Williams's observation about normalization.

item.title: A reader points Rosen to Question Everything
item.description: After a reader recommends KCRW's interview with Barton Gellman, Rosen praises The Journalist and the Firefighter and its follow-up as a rethinking of journalism he had hoped to hear.

item.title: Question Everything and a rethink of journalism
item.description: Rosen recommends KCRW's The Journalist and the Firefighter and its follow-up, praising the staff of Question Everything and Barton Gellman.

item.title: 60 Minutes and the Washington Post
item.description: Rosen shares the Guardian's report on a former 60 Minutes editor's account of the program's destruction. He compares it with the Washington Post while distinguishing their prior business conditions.

item.title: The media frenzy around Hasan Piker
item.description: Rosen points readers to Status, where he contributed a comment about the media attention surrounding Hasan Piker.

item.title: Bangor Daily News states what its journalism stands for
item.description: Rosen returns to the Bangor Daily News values statement and highlights its refusal to be impartial about harms such as corruption, racism, and government incompetence.

item.title: Truth Social mentions as unpaid promotion
item.description: Rosen shares an Editor and Publisher argument that news stories leading with Trump's Truth Social posts also promote a company controlled by their subject.

item.title: How far Bangor Daily News moves beyond impartiality
item.description: Responding to criticism that the Bangor Daily News values statement is too vague, Rosen says it makes progress in some areas while remaining limited in others.

item.title: The pull of journalism's industry consensus
item.description: In the discussion of the Bangor Daily News values statement, Rosen explains its limits as a desire to remain within the industry's consensus.

item.title: Bangor Daily News and the view from nowhere
item.description: Rosen highlights the Bangor Daily News statement of journalistic values as an attempt to find an alternative to the view from nowhere.

item.title: Reporting on the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident
item.description: Rosen shares accounts from Dwarkesh Patel and Platformer about OpenAI and Hugging Face, describing the reporting as startling and accessible.

item.title: Opinion writers, audiences, and newsroom managers
item.description: Rosen argues that opinion writers with their own brands and audiences limit managers' power. He recommends Eric Deggans's account of why Karen Attiah's victory matters.

item.title: A reader's comparison with George Lakoff
item.description: A reader compares Rosen's approach to election stakes with George Lakoff's moral framing. Rosen replies that he has not met Lakoff but sees similarities in their approaches.

item.title: A media studies doctorate and a journalism teaching career
item.description: Replying to a reader who connected his media criticism with political analysis, Rosen explains that his media studies doctorate and journalism work could coexist in NYU's Arts and Sciences program.

item.title: Two weeks of reading for a journalism course
item.description: Rosen proposes beginning a journalism course with Tom Rosenstiel and The Elements of Journalism, followed by The Next Journalism: How the Press Must Change to Serve Democracy.

item.title: Election coverage: The stakes beyond the polls
item.description: Rosen points to Mike Podhorzer's midterm overview as an example of election coverage organized around consequences rather than winning probabilities.

item.title: Karen Attiah's account of the Washington Post
item.description: Rosen recommends Karen Attiah's Columbia Journalism Review interview and calls her account damaging to the Washington Post.
